title: Choosing Between RDS and DynamoDB
description: Compare relational and NoSQL databases on AWS and match them to ASP.NET Core application requirements.

data.text: Choosing the right database affects application complexity, performance, and cost. RDS and DynamoDB serve different purposes, and understanding their strengths helps you make the right choice.

rows: Vertical scaling with some read replicas

items: **Choose RDS** when you need complex queries, joins, transactions, or existing SQL Server skills
**Choose DynamoDB** when you need serverless scaling, single-digit millisecond latency, or flexible schemas
**Use both** — RDS for transactional data and DynamoDB for high-throughput access patterns

items.question: Can I use EF Core with DynamoDB?
items.answer: EF Core is designed for relational databases. Use the `AWSSDK.DynamoDBv2` client directly, or consider a third-party DynamoDB ORM like `DynamoDBContext`.

items.question: Is DynamoDB more expensive than RDS?
items.answer: For unpredictable or spiky workloads, DynamoDB can be cheaper because you pay per request. For steady workloads, RDS reserved instances are often more cost-effective.

data.title: Quick Reference
points: DynamoDB = NoSQL key-value and document data
RDS = fixed capacity with scaling options
data.takeaway: Most ASP.NET Core apps start with RDS for relational data and add DynamoDB for specific high-throughput or serverless use cases.
